lines.text: Why this matters
Storage format is not a cosmetic file-extension choice. It changes how much data an analytical engine
must read, how types are represented, how well repeated values compress, and whether later tools can
skip work. CSV remains useful for interchange and inspection, but an analytics pipeline that repeatedly
scans a few columns from wide data benefits from a columnar format such as Parquet.
Picture it in your head
Picture eight order cards. A row-oriented layout keeps every field for card 1 together, then every field
for card 2. A columnar layout groups all order IDs, then all dates, then all regions, then all amounts.
Parquet is not literally one file per column: it splits rows into row groups and stores each column
together inside each row group. That hybrid detail matters later when we discuss skipping.
New words before we use them
row-oriented = values for one record stay together; columnar = values for one field stay together within
a storage unit; OLTP = workloads that often read/update individual records; OLAP = analytical
scans/aggregations; Parquet = self-describing columnar file format; projection = choose only required
columns.

Follow with me once
Open `practice/data/orders.csv`. It has six business columns and eight order rows. Imagine a report that
needs only `region` and `amount`. A simple CSV reader still parses every field in every row. A
Parquet-capable engine can request only the column chunks it needs. In the pure-Python simulator we
count this as a conceptual 48 cell-values available versus 16 projected values. That count is a mental
model, not a benchmark claim about bytes or speed.
python practice/storage_sim/storage_reasoning_simulator.py --section layout # Optional learner-PC real
Parquet lab after installing pyarrow: python practice/parquet/parquet_lab.py --section build
What you should see
The simulator reports 8 rows x 6 columns = 48 logical source cells and a two-column projection of 16
logical values. The optional PyArrow lab writes a real Parquet file from the same fixture and prints its
schema. Do not claim a performance multiplier from this tiny classroom dataset.
Break it / common failure
The tempting slogan 'Parquet is always faster' is too broad. Reading a single tiny record, ingesting
streaming bytes, or exchanging data with a simple external system can favor other formats. The
engineering question is workload + access pattern + interoperability, not fashion.
Reason through a realistic incident
A teammate converts a 20 KB configuration export to Parquet because 'all data engineering uses
Parquet.' The pipeline becomes more complex without reducing meaningful cost. Explain why format
choice should follow access pattern and scale.
Deepen the engineering reasoning
A useful way to choose a storage format is to separate three questions. First, what is the unit of access:
one record, a small keyed set, or a scan across many records? Second, which fields are usually needed:
nearly all columns or only a narrow subset? Third, who must read the data and with which tools? A
transactional database can be excellent for point updates even though a columnar file is excellent for
analytical scans. CSV can be a sensible interchange format even though it lacks Parquet's typed column
metadata. Parquet earns its place when analytical engines repeatedly scan large datasets and can
benefit from projection, compression and metadata-aware reads. That is why 'Parquet is faster' is an
incomplete sentence; faster for which operation, on which engine, at what scale? In this module, keep
logical correctness separate from physical efficiency. If two files contain the same eight valid orders and
reconcile to the same 1100 amount total, they can be logically equivalent while having very different
scan cost. Later, Spark will make that distinction visible through distributed reads. For now, the
professional habit is to write the workload before choosing the format: expected row count, columns
commonly selected, update pattern, retention, interoperability and the engine that will consume it. This
prevents format choice from becoming cargo-cult architecture.
Why the professional version is safer
Use Parquet when typed columnar analytical reads, compression and ecosystem interoperability matter.
Keep source/raw evidence when the pipeline contract requires it; converting to Parquet is a new
representation, not proof that the original source is no longer needed.
Now you do a changed version alone
For three workloads - point lookup of one customer, nightly sum of `amount` by region across millions of
rows, and a vendor handoff to a nontechnical partner - choose row-oriented database/CSV/Parquet and
defend the trade-off. Then state what Parquet buys the nightly analytical case.
Fresh changed retry
A report now needs all six columns for only two rows rather than two columns for all rows. Explain why
the columnar advantage is less obvious and why file format alone cannot answer the performance
question.
Validation and recovery ladder
State the logical grain/table version/physical unit you are reasoning about before changing
anything.
Separate logical correctness from physical layout: rows/keys/totals first, then files/row
groups/partitions/versions.
Inspect the smallest evidence that can falsify your assumption: metadata fixture, file manifest, log
version, source-key uniqueness or schema contract.
Open the Explained Review only after saving a genuine attempt; reveal only the weak concept.
Close review and solve the changed retry. Preserve the original attempt and the independent
validation.
Ready-made revision
Use Parquet when typed columnar analytical reads, compression and ecosystem interoperability matter.
Keep source/raw evidence when the pipeline contract requires it; converting to Parquet is a new
representation, not proof that the original source is no longer needed.

Save your command/design, actual observed output or error, one independent control, a 60-90 second
explain-back, and the changed retry. If this lesson needs native Parquet/Delta-engine evidence you
have not run, label that part PENDING rather than claiming a simulator/static PASS is a native runtime

Why this matters
Calling Parquet 'columnar' is not enough to debug real reads. A Parquet file contains row groups; each
row group contains one column chunk per column; column chunks contain pages; the footer stores
schema and metadata that let readers locate data and inspect statistics. This structure is why a reader
can avoid touching some bytes.
Picture it in your head
Picture a library with two floors. Each floor contains shelves for order_id, date, region and amount for
only the rows assigned to that floor. The catalogue at the exit lists where each shelf is and summary
facts such as the minimum and maximum amount. The reader opens the catalogue first, then visits only
relevant shelves/floors.
New words before we use them
row group = horizontal batch of rows inside a Parquet file; column chunk = one column's values for one
row group; page = smaller encoded/compressed unit inside a column chunk; footer = file metadata
written after data; statistics = metadata such as min/max/null count when available.

Follow with me once
Our metadata fixture deliberately models two row groups: RG0 covers 2026-09-01 through 2026-09-02
with amount 80-200; RG1 covers 2026-09-03 through 2026-09-04 with amount 90-190. A date filter `>=
2026-09-03` can prove RG0 is impossible. An amount filter `> 195` can prove RG1 is impossible. The
fixture is clearly labelled as a course metadata simulation; the optional PyArrow lab inspects real
metadata when PyArrow is available.
python practice/storage_sim/storage_reasoning_simulator.py --section metadata
python practice/parquet/parquet_lab.py --section metadata  # requires pyarrow
What you should see
The simulator prints two row groups and identifies which group can be skipped for each supplied
predicate. On the learner PC, the real Parquet lab should show 8 rows, 2 row groups
(row_group_size=4), schema fields, and per-row-group amount/date statistics when written by the
pinned PyArrow runtime.
Break it / common failure
Min/max metadata is not a magical index. If each row group contains the full value range, min/max
cannot exclude anything. Statistics can also be absent or affected by writer/format details. Never
promise data skipping from a file extension alone.
Reason through a realistic incident
A query filters `amount > 150`, but every row group has min 1 and max 10,000 because records arrived
randomly. The team expected row-group skipping and gets little. Diagnose the difference between
'metadata exists' and 'metadata is selective.'
Deepen the engineering reasoning
Parquet metadata is useful because it lets an engine reason about a file before decoding every value.
Think in layers. The file has a schema that says which fields exist and their types. The file is divided into
row groups; each row group covers a horizontal slice of rows. Inside a row group, each column is stored
as a column chunk. Metadata can include row counts, encodings and statistics such as minimum,
maximum and null count. Those statistics are not the business truth by themselves; they are evidence
an engine may use to avoid work. In our fixture, row group 0 covers dates 2026-09-01 through
2026-09-02 and row group 1 covers 2026-09-03 through 2026-09-04. A filter for dates from 2026-09-03
onward can therefore identify row group 0 as impossible before reading its values. But statistics have
limits: missing statistics, broad min/max ranges, encrypted metadata, unsupported predicates or data
distributions can prevent useful skipping. Also distinguish schema from business contract. A Parquet
field typed as string does not prove that every customer_id is a valid customer. Physical metadata helps
readers plan work; quality rules still belong to the pipeline. When you inspect metadata, record what it
can prove, what it only suggests and what still requires reading/validation. That three-column habit -
prove / suggest / cannot answer - is a practical way to avoid overclaiming from file metadata.
Why the professional version is safer
Treat row-group statistics as observable evidence used by a reader/planner, not as a guarantee. Inspect
real file metadata when diagnosing scan behavior and keep the logical predicate separate from the
physical skipping opportunity.
Now you do a changed version alone
Using `parquet_metadata_fixture.json`, decide which row groups could be skipped for (a) `order_date
>= 2026-09-03`, (b) `amount > 195`, and (c) `region = 'East'` when the fixture has no region min/max.
Explain exactly what evidence supports each decision.
Fresh changed retry
Change the amount predicate to `amount >= 90`. Re-evaluate both row groups and explain why a less
selective boundary changes skipping even though the physical file did not change.

Why this matters
Analytical efficiency usually combines two separate ideas: projection reduces columns read;
predicate/data skipping reduces chunks or row groups considered. Beginners often mix these up and
say a `WHERE` clause means the engine read only matching rows. It might still read a row group and
filter rows after decode.
Picture it in your head
Projection is choosing which shelves to visit. Predicate skipping is deciding an entire floor cannot
possibly contain the requested book. Row-level filtering is checking individual books after entering a
floor. Those are three different stages.
New words before we use them
column pruning/projection = do not read unrequested columns; predicate pushdown = pass a filter
toward the data source/reader; data skipping = avoid files/row groups using metadata; residual filter =
condition still evaluated after data is read/decoded.

Follow with me once
For `SELECT order_id, amount FROM orders WHERE order_date >= '2026-09-03'`, the desired columns
are `order_id`, `amount`, plus whatever the engine needs to evaluate `order_date`. The fixture says
RG0 ends on Sep 2, so it can be skipped; RG1 remains. This does not mean only final qualifying rows
were physically read from RG1.
python practice/storage_sim/storage_reasoning_simulator.py --section reads # Learner-PC PyArrow projection
example: python practice/parquet/parquet_lab.py --section projection
What you should see
The simulator separates `columns_requested` from `row_groups_candidate`. For the date predicate,
RG0 is excluded and RG1 remains. The optional PyArrow read returns only the requested output
columns while the filter behavior is inspected separately.
Break it / common failure
A common wrong proof is timing one tiny local query and concluding predicate pushdown works. OS
cache, tiny data, engine overhead and different physical layout can dominate. Better evidence is
metadata, query plan/scan metrics on a capable engine, and controlled comparisons.
Reason through a realistic incident
A dashboard selects only `order_id` and `amount`, but a developer wraps the Parquet read in code that
first loads every column into pandas and then slices two columns. Explain why the final DataFrame
shape does not prove column pruning occurred.
Deepen the engineering reasoning
Projection and predicate pushdown are often mentioned together, but they solve different kinds of
wasted work. Projection reduces the columns requested. Predicate pushdown lets a filter reach the scan
layer so the reader can use partition or file statistics to avoid data that cannot match. Row-group
skipping is one possible consequence when metadata proves a whole row group fails the predicate.
Imagine a report that needs order_id and amount for dates on or after 2026-09-03. Projection asks for
two output columns, although the filter column order_date may still be read or inspected to evaluate the
filter. Predicate reasoning compares the date condition with metadata and may skip earlier row groups.
The important boundary is that 'pushdown happened' and 'data was skipped' are not synonyms. An
engine can push a predicate but still need to read every group because the metadata ranges overlap
the filter. Conversely, partition pruning can skip whole directories before Parquet row-group logic starts.
When debugging a slow read, ask in order: Did I select unnecessary columns? Is the filter expressed in a
form the engine can push? Does the physical layout provide useful statistics or partitions? Is the dataset
so small that overhead dominates anyway? In later Spark work you will inspect plans and metrics. Here,
mastery means you can predict which physical units are candidates and then validate that prediction
instead of treating optimization terms as magic incantations.
Why the professional version is safer
Design schemas and file layout so common analytical filters have useful metadata and common
projections avoid wide reads. Verify with engine evidence; SQL syntax expresses intent but does not by
itself prove physical I/O.

Why this matters
Compression and compaction solve different problems. Compression reduces bytes inside files.
Compaction reduces the number of files by rewriting many small files into fewer larger files. A directory
containing 10,000 tiny, well-compressed files can still be expensive to list, plan and open.
Picture it in your head
Compression is vacuum-packing each suitcase. Compaction is replacing hundreds of tiny suitcases with
a few appropriately sized ones. Vacuum-packing does not reduce how many suitcases the airport must
tag and handle.
New words before we use them
codec = compression algorithm such as Snappy/ZSTD/GZIP; encoding = representation such as
dictionary/RLE before/alongside compression; small-file problem = operational/query overhead from
many tiny files; compaction = rewrite into fewer larger files; OPTIMIZE = Databricks table-layout rewrite
operation.

Follow with me once
The supplied manifest contains six tiny files totaling 65 MB. The compaction planner groups them into
one logical target under a 128 MB classroom target. The output explicitly says it is a planning
simulation; it does not pretend `OPTIMIZE` ran. Current Databricks docs also note that an OPTIMIZE
rewrite creates new files while older unreferenced files can remain physically present until
retention/VACUUM permits cleanup.
python practice/storage_sim/storage_reasoning_simulator.py --section compaction # Read
practice/data/small_files_manifest.json
What you should see
The planner reports 6 source files / 65 MB and one proposed compacted group. Logical row/amount
controls must remain identical before and after the plan. The plan changes physical layout, not business
content.
Break it / common failure
Do not set one universal 'perfect file size' and cargo-cult it across engines/workloads. Target sizes,
automatic tuning and clustering features vary. Also do not call deleting files 'compaction' - compaction
is a rewrite preserving logical data.
Reason through a realistic incident
An engineer gzips 5,000 tiny JSON files and celebrates a 70% storage reduction, yet Spark query
planning remains slow. Explain why fewer bytes and fewer file-open/listing operations are separate
axes.
Deepen the engineering reasoning
Small-file problems are a systems problem, not merely a file-size aesthetic. Each file can add listing,
planning, metadata and open/close overhead. Thousands of tiny files can therefore make a dataset
expensive to discover and schedule even when the total number of bytes is modest. Compaction
rewrites many small files into fewer larger files while preserving the logical table content. That
preservation requirement is why reconciliation belongs in a storage lesson: row count, key count and
trusted amount total must match before and after the rewrite. Compression is related but different.
Compression reduces bytes using encodings/codecs; compaction changes file layout and file count. A
compressed tiny-file swarm can still be a small-file problem. Likewise, one gigantic file can reduce file
count but hurt parallelism, recovery granularity or write behavior. The correct target is workload- and
platform-dependent. Our classroom manifest deliberately uses six tiny logical files totaling 65 MB and a
128 MB teaching target to make the reasoning visible, not to decree a universal production number. In a
real platform, inspect the engine's recommendations, workload concurrency, partitioning, write
frequency and downstream scan sizes. Also remember that table formats may keep old files after
compaction for time travel until retention cleanup. Seeing storage usage temporarily increase after
OPTIMIZE-like maintenance is therefore not automatically a leak. First identify active files versus
retained historical files, then reconcile the logical table.
Why the professional version is safer
Measure file count, typical file size, partition distribution and query behavior before tuning. Prefer
platform-managed optimization where appropriate, but understand the invariant: physical rewrites must
preserve logical rows/keys/totals.

Why this matters
Partitioning can eliminate entire directory/table slices when filters align with the partition key, but too
many partitions create metadata and small-file overhead and can prevent compaction across
boundaries. A timestamp/customer/order ID is usually a poor partition key because its cardinality can
explode.
Picture it in your head
A partition is a labeled room. 'year=2026/month=09' creates a few useful rooms.
'customer_id=C000001' creates a room for every customer. If most rooms contain one shoebox, the
warehouse is organized but inefficient.
New words before we use them
partition column = field used to divide physical storage; cardinality = number of distinct values;
partition pruning = skip partitions using partition values; over-partitioning = too many tiny partitions;
clustering = alternative physical organization used by some platforms.

Partitioning vs over-partitioning; current alternatives

Follow with me once
Our eight-row fixture has four distinct dates and four regions but eight order IDs. The simulator
compares partition counts for date, region and order_id and calculates rows per partition. The point is
not that date is always correct - only that high-cardinality keys can create one-row directories quickly.
Current Databricks guidance increasingly prefers liquid clustering for many managed tables, so
partitioning should be a deliberate choice rather than an automatic ritual.
python practice/storage_sim/storage_reasoning_simulator.py --section partitioning
What you should see
The simulator shows 4 date partitions, 4 region partitions and 8 order_id partitions for only 8 rows.
`order_id` therefore has one row/partition in the fixture. You should be able to explain why that pattern
scales badly.
Break it / common failure
Do not choose a partition key only because users filter it sometimes. Estimate distinct values, data per
partition, filter selectivity, write pattern and maintenance behavior. A high-cardinality timestamp can
create vast numbers of tiny directories/files.
Reason through a realistic incident
A table is partitioned by `event_timestamp` down to seconds. Every batch creates thousands of
almost-empty partitions, and compaction cannot combine across them. Explain the root design error
and a safer alternative category.
Deepen the engineering reasoning
Partitioning is valuable when a filter can eliminate large groups of data cheaply, but a partition key is
not automatically good because it appears in WHERE clauses. Cardinality and distribution matter.
Partitioning eight classroom rows by order_id would create eight nearly empty partitions: the directory
layout becomes an index made of folders, with overhead and no useful grouping. A date key can also be
too fine if the table is small or the workload rarely filters by date. Region has lower cardinality in our
fixture, but that still does not make it universally best; if nearly every query scans all regions, the
partition directories add complexity without pruning benefit. A professional partition decision includes
expected table size, common filters, cardinality, skew, ingestion pattern and maintenance behavior.
Modern lakehouse engines can also use clustering or data-skipping features that reduce the need for
rigid directory partitioning, so avoid copying old Hive-era rules blindly. Before creating a partition
column, estimate how many partitions exist per retention window and approximately how much data
lands in each. Then imagine the smallest common query: how many partitions would it touch? Finally
consider writes: will late data or updates repeatedly hit many partitions? If the answers look messy, test
an unpartitioned or differently clustered design. Partitioning is physical layout, not a business grain.
Changing it should not alter the row/key/amount truth of the table; always keep those logical controls
separate.
Why the professional version is safer
Partitioning is a physical optimization contract. Keep partition cardinality and files-per-partition
observable; do not let an old layout silently become a new bottleneck as volume and query patterns
change.

Why this matters
A data lake, warehouse and lakehouse are architecture patterns with different storage/management
assumptions, not job titles or product slogans. The useful question is where raw/open files live, where
governed tables live, what transaction/quality guarantees exist, and which engines can read the data.
Picture it in your head
A lake is a large storage yard that can keep many shapes of raw cargo. A warehouse has catalogued
shelves and controlled receiving rules. A lakehouse adds a table-management layer over object/file
storage so data can retain open-file economics while gaining stronger table semantics. Real platforms
blend these ideas, so the boundaries are architectural, not perfectly pure.
New words before we use them
data lake = scalable file/object storage for varied data; warehouse = managed analytical database/table
system; lakehouse = architecture adding warehouse-like table management/transactions/governance
over lake-style storage; open format = format readable by multiple compatible engines; medallion =
Bronze/Silver/Gold layering pattern.

Official: Databricks - What is a data lakehouse?
Lake vs warehouse vs lakehouse role
OPEN SOURCE - CLICK HERE
https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/lakehouse/
Follow with me once
Use one pipeline: vendor CSV lands unchanged, standardized typed records become Silver-like data,
and a business aggregate becomes Gold-like serving data. In a lake-only design those may be files plus
conventions. In a warehouse, managed tables and SQL engine rules dominate. In a lakehouse,
Parquet-backed table formats such as Delta add a transaction/table layer over object storage.
python practice/storage_sim/storage_reasoning_simulator.py --section architecture
What you should see
The simulator prints the same data flow under three architecture lenses and asks which layer owns
schema, transactions and serving contracts. There is no score for choosing a fashionable label; the
answer must state storage, table semantics and consumers.
Break it / common failure
Do not claim 'lakehouse replaces every warehouse' or 'lake means ungoverned mess.' Governance and
modeling depend on implementation. Also do not call a folder of Parquet files a transactional table
merely because a SQL engine can query them.
Reason through a realistic incident
A team says its S3 folder of Parquet files is a lakehouse because BI can query it. No transaction log or
managed table state exists. Explain what capability is missing from that claim and what could still be
true about the folder.
Deepen the engineering reasoning
Lake, warehouse and lakehouse are architectural roles, not three mutually exclusive product boxes. A
data lake traditionally emphasizes low-cost object/file storage and open or semi-open file formats,
making it easy to retain raw and diverse data. A warehouse traditionally emphasizes managed tables,
SQL semantics, governance and strong performance for curated analytics. A lakehouse tries to keep
object/file storage economics and openness while adding table semantics such as transactions, schema
controls, history and governance. The mistake is to reduce the comparison to 'cheap versus fast' or 'old
versus new.' Real organizations often use more than one pattern, and cloud warehouses themselves can
read external files while lakehouse systems can expose warehouse-like SQL endpoints. For a design
decision, ask what guarantees are required: concurrent writers, transaction consistency, data sharing,
fine-grained governance, BI latency, open-format access, multi-engine interoperability and operational

Why this matters
Parquet gives efficient files but not, by itself, a safe multi-file table transaction. Delta Lake adds a
transaction log that records which data files constitute each committed table version. Readers use a
consistent snapshot; writers commit changes atomically through the log rather than asking every reader
to infer table state from a directory listing.
Picture it in your head
Imagine a restaurant inventory made of boxes plus an official ledger. The boxes are Parquet data files.
The ledger says which boxes are active in version 0, then which boxes were added/removed in version
1. A reader trusts one committed ledger page, not whatever loose boxes happen to be visible
mid-delivery.
New words before we use them
transaction log = ordered record of table actions/commits; snapshot = table state at one committed
version; ACID = atomicity, consistency, isolation, durability; optimistic concurrency = writers
validate/commit against shared state; data file = physical Parquet file referenced by table state.

Break it / common failure
Never edit Parquet files or `_delta_log` internals by hand as a normal repair strategy. A table format's
guarantees depend on coordinated log + data-file semantics. Random file deletion can corrupt the table
or destroy time-travel capability.
Reason through a realistic incident
An operator deletes an 'old-looking' Parquet file directly from a Delta table directory to save storage. A
historical query later fails. Explain why the filesystem view was not sufficient evidence that the file was
safe to delete.
Deepen the engineering reasoning
The transaction log is the key mental bridge from 'files in a directory' to 'a table with versions.' In a
Delta-style design, a successful write does not mean 'overwrite some Parquet files and hope readers
catch a consistent moment.' Instead, the table records an ordered commit describing which data files
are active, which were removed from the current snapshot, and metadata about the operation. Readers
reconstruct a table version from committed log state. That is why a new snapshot can become visible
atomically even though multiple physical files may be involved. ACID still needs precise language.
Atomicity means a commit is visible as a unit; consistency means declared invariants/constraints and
table rules are preserved; isolation concerns concurrent operations seeing sensible states; durability
means committed state survives expected failures. Do not claim that a transaction log makes every
upstream business rule correct. The log can faithfully commit duplicate customer IDs if your pipeline
allows them. Our simulator intentionally records version, operation, active snapshot, row count, unique
keys and amount total so you can see the control plane, but it is not the Delta engine. Use it to reason
about commit boundaries and history. Later, when running real Delta, compare the engine's history/log
behavior with this mental model and note where implementation details are richer than the simulator.
Why the professional version is safer
Treat the transaction log as table metadata/state, not optional bookkeeping. Use supported table
APIs/commands so file rewrites, metadata and versions stay coherent.

Why this matters
MERGE is a table-level way to reconcile a source change set with current target state: matched keys can
update/delete and unmatched keys can insert. The hardest part is not syntax; it is proving the source
has an unambiguous row for each target key and that rerunning the change set produces the intended
state.
Picture it in your head
Picture a clerk with a current customer/order card file and a change envelope. For each change, the
clerk finds the matching card or creates a new one. If the envelope contains two contradictory changes
for the same card, the clerk needs a rule before touching the cabinet.
New words before we use them
upsert = update existing key or insert new key; MERGE = conditional matched/not-matched table
operation; business key = identity used for match; source deduplication = ensure source row/key rule is
unambiguous; current-state table = one intended latest row per key.

Break it / common failure
`MERGE` is not a license to skip source-grain checks. A source with duplicate business keys can be
ambiguous and may error or produce wrong current-state logic depending on engine/rules. `DISTINCT`
is not a universal repair because two different updates can remain genuinely conflicting.
Reason through a realistic incident
A CDC batch contains two records for O1003 with different event times. A developer drops duplicates
without ordering and MERGEs the survivor. Explain why 'one row per key' is necessary but not sufficient;
the survivor-selection rule must also reflect business/event semantics.
Deepen the engineering reasoning
MERGE is powerful because one statement can express current-state changes, but its safety begins
before the statement runs. First define the target key and confirm the source batch has at most one
intended row per key. If source O1003 appears twice with conflicting amounts, 'last row wins' is not a
neutral technical choice; it silently invents a precedence rule. That is why the simulator blocks the
duplicate-key source instead of resolving it arbitrarily. Next classify matched and not-matched behavior.
In our clean batch, O1003 and O1005 are updates and O1009 is an insert. The expected current state is
nine unique keys totaling 1250. These three controls - update/insert counts, key uniqueness, and
reconciled total - give independent evidence that the MERGE did what the business rule intended.
Idempotency also needs thought. Reapplying the same current-state source should converge to the
same result when the operation is designed correctly, but event-style data may require a different
append/deduplicate rule. Do not use MERGE as a universal ingestion hammer. It is appropriate when the
target model and source semantics support update/insert matching. In production, also reason about
deletion/tombstone rules, late-arriving records, sequence/version columns and concurrent writers. A
syntactically valid MERGE can be semantically wrong if the match key or precedence rule is wrong.
Why the professional version is safer
Make MERGE deterministic at the source boundary and idempotent for reruns. Reconcile affected
keys/counts/totals and keep change-event evidence when the business requires history.

Why this matters
Schema enforcement protects a table from accidental incompatible writes; schema evolution is the
deliberate process of changing that contract. The safe mindset is 'fail or route unknown change until
policy approves it,' not 'turn on auto-merge and accept whatever arrives.'
Picture it in your head
Think of an airport baggage gauge. Enforcement checks whether a bag meets today's allowed shape.
Evolution is management changing the gauge and policy for tomorrow. Quietly sawing the gauge wider
every time a bag fails is not governance.
New words before we use them
schema enforcement = reject writes that violate table contract; evolution = intentional contract change;
additive column = new field; rename/drop = semantic changes that can break consumers; type
widening = move to compatible broader type under supported rules; compatibility = whether existing
readers/writers continue to work.

What you should see
Approved additive evolution creates version 2 with `source_system` present and 9 keys / total 1250.
Incompatible numeric-type input is rejected; history does not gain a successful commit for that bad
write.
Break it / common failure
A new nullable column can be low-risk; renaming a field used by downstream jobs is not. Some
platforms support automatic evolution for specific change classes, but support does not mean the
business meaning is safe. Schema compatibility is both technical and contractual.
Reason through a realistic incident
Upstream renames `customer_id` to `client_id`. Auto-evolution treats it as a new column while the old
field becomes null for new records. The pipeline keeps running but joins collapse. Explain why
operational success can hide semantic breakage.
Deepen the engineering reasoning
Schema enforcement and evolution should be treated as contract management. Enforcement protects
the current trusted shape; evolution changes that trusted shape deliberately. The safest workflow is
detect -> classify -> approve -> migrate/test consumers -> commit the change. An additive nullable
column such as source_system is often easier because old readers can ignore it and old rows can
remain null/defaulted. A rename from customer_id to client_id is different: a naive auto-evolution can
create a new field while downstream joins still reference the old name, producing valid files but invalid
business results. Type changes also need semantic review. Integer to wider numeric may be technically
supported, while string to struct changes how every consumer reads the value. The engine's capability
is only one input to the decision. Keep a schema contract that identifies required fields, types,
nullability, key semantics and owners. When a producer drifts unexpectedly, quarantine or fail the
affected records/run according to policy rather than coercing values until the job turns green. Then test
important downstream models. Our simulator demonstrates one approved additive field and one
incompatible amount value. The important evidence is not merely that the good case succeeded and
bad case failed; it is that the rejected write did not advance table version or corrupt the trusted current
state. State preservation after failure is part of the contract.
Why the professional version is safer
Version schema contracts. Prefer explicit, reviewed evolution for important tables. Test downstream
compatibility and keep rescue/quarantine paths for unexpected producer changes rather than silently
coercing them into trusted data.

Why this matters
Time travel is possible because table versions reference historical files. Retention and VACUUM decide
how long old physical files remain available. Therefore 'history row exists' and 'old version is still
queryable' are related but not identical promises. Maintenance must balance audit/recovery needs
against storage cleanup.
Picture it in your head
The transaction log is a photo album index; old data files are the actual photos. Keeping the index entry
but shredding the photo means you can know an old version existed without being able to reconstruct
every byte of it. VACUUM is a controlled cleanup, not a casual delete command.
New words before we use them
time travel = query an earlier table version/timestamp when required files remain; retention = policy for
keeping old files/history; VACUUM = remove no-longer-referenced old files beyond retention; DRY RUN
= preview deletion candidates; Bronze/Silver/Gold = raw-ish -> validated -> serving layer pattern.

What you should see

Break it / common failure
Do not treat VACUUM as a performance command that can be run with arbitrarily tiny retention.
Removing old files can permanently eliminate time-travel/recovery capability and can be dangerous for
long-running jobs. Also distinguish `OPTIMIZE` (rewrite layout) from `VACUUM` (remove eligible unused
files).
Reason through a realistic incident
A team compacts a table, sees storage grow because new compacted files coexist with old ones, then
immediately runs aggressive VACUUM with safety disabled. Explain the lifecycle and why the second
reaction can destroy legitimate rollback/recovery windows.
Deepen the engineering reasoning
Time travel, retention and VACUUM form one lifecycle. A table version can be described by history
metadata, but reconstructing that version requires the underlying data files to remain available.
Retention policy therefore converts a business recovery requirement into storage behavior. If finance
needs reproducible month-close states for 30 days, a seven-day file-retention window is insufficient
even if seven days is a common/default platform safety threshold. The correct retention is the maximum
of operational safety and business/compliance recovery needs, within platform constraints. Before
cleanup, inspect history and identify long-running readers or restore requirements. Use DRY RUN where
available to see candidates. After cleanup, validate the current table and document what historical
recovery window remains. Also separate maintenance commands. OPTIMIZE/compaction rewrites active
layout for read efficiency; VACUUM removes old no-longer-referenced files after retention. Running
compaction can temporarily increase storage because both new active files and retained old files
coexist. Aggressive VACUUM immediately afterward may save bytes while destroying rollback evidence.
The Bronze/Silver/Gold checkpoint at the end of M11 ties these ideas together: Bronze preserves source
evidence, Silver applies validated contracts and deduplication, Gold serves business-ready models.
Those names are useful only when each layer has explicit grain, schema, quality, retention and
reconciliation rules.
Why the professional version is safer
Make retention a business/recovery policy, not a random storage tweak. Use table-supported
maintenance commands, preserve evidence of changes, and connect Bronze/Silver/Gold layers with
explicit contracts and reconciliation rather than names alone.
